cbt_desc_1: Cognitive distortions are exaggerated or irrational thought patterns that can reinforce negative thinking and emotions. They were first identified by Dr. Aaron Beck and popularized by Dr. David Burns in the context of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
cbt_desc_2: Everyone experiences them from time to time. The goal of this journal is not to eliminate them — it's to notice them, name them, and challenge them. By bringing awareness to your thinking patterns, you can gradually shift toward more balanced, realistic perspectives.
cbt_cycle: Thoughts → Feelings → Behaviors → (reinforces) Thoughts. By interrupting the thought at the top of the cycle, you change everything downstream.
cbt_0_desc: Expecting the worst-case scenario to happen, even when there's little evidence. You blow things out of proportion and assume disaster is inevitable.
cbt_0_example: I made a mistake in my presentation — my boss probably thinks I'm incompetent and I'll get fired.
cbt_1_desc: Seeing situations in only two categories instead of on a spectrum. Things are either perfect or a total failure, with nothing in between.
cbt_1_example: If I don't get an A on this exam, I'm a complete failure as a student.
cbt_2_desc: Taking a single negative event and seeing it as a never-ending pattern of defeat. Words like "always," "never," and "every time" are red flags.
cbt_2_example: I didn't get a reply to my text — nobody ever wants to talk to me.
cbt_3_desc: Dwelling exclusively on one negative detail while ignoring all the positive aspects of a situation.
cbt_3_example: My performance review had nine positive comments and one suggestion — and I can't stop thinking about that one thing.
cbt_4_desc: Assuming you know what others are thinking about you, usually negatively, without any real evidence.
cbt_4_example: My friend didn't wave back — she must be angry with me.
cbt_5_desc: Predicting a negative outcome will happen and treating that prediction as an established fact.
cbt_5_example: I'm going to embarrass myself at the party, so there's no point in going.
cbt_6_desc: Believing that because you feel a certain way, it must be true. Feelings are treated as facts.
cbt_6_example: I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong.
cbt_7_desc: Attaching a global, negative label to yourself or others based on a single event, instead of describing the specific behavior.
cbt_7_example: I forgot to call my mom — I'm a terrible son.
cbt_8_desc: Taking responsibility for events that are not entirely under your control, or blaming yourself for external circumstances.
cbt_8_example: My child is struggling in school — I must be a bad parent.
cbt_9_desc: Holding yourself to rigid rules about how you or others "should" or "must" behave. These create guilt and frustration when reality doesn't match.
cbt_9_example: I should be more productive. I must not waste any time today.
cbt_10_desc: Rejecting positive experiences by insisting they don't count. You maintain a negative belief despite evidence to the contrary.
cbt_10_example: They only said they liked my work because they're being nice — they don't really mean it.
cbt_11_desc: Exaggerating the importance of negative events or your flaws (magnification) and shrinking the importance of positive events or your strengths (minimization).
cbt_11_example: Getting one question wrong proves I'm bad at math. Getting the other 19 right doesn't mean anything.
howto_intro: DailyMood is a private, encrypted journal that helps you track your mood, emotions, and thoughts over time. Everything stays on your machine.
howto_entries_text: Click "New Entry" in the top bar or on the Journal page. Fill in the title, date, and time. Use the mood slider to rate your day (0 = Terrible, 6 = Amazing). If you have created custom scales, their sliders appear here too. Select tags by clicking them, write your thoughts in the body, and optionally enable reflection prompts. Click "Save Entry" when done.
howto_scales_text: Go to Settings > Custom Scales. Click "Add" to create a new scale (e.g. "Anxiety" 0-10 or "Energy" 0-5). Once created, these sliders appear on every new entry. Remove scales anytime with the x button. Scale data appears as bar charts in the Stats page.
howto_tags_text: Tags are pre-defined labels you attach to entries for filtering later. Go to Settings > Tags to manage your tag list. Each language has its own independent tag set. When writing an entry, just click the tags you want to include.
howto_calendar_text: The Journal page shows a monthly calendar. Each day with an entry shows a colored dot matching your mood. Click a day to see its entries below. Double-click a day to create a new entry for that date. Use the arrow buttons to navigate months.
howto_export_text: Go to Settings > Export to download all your entries as a .tar.gz or .zip archive. Use Export as PDF to compile entries into a single PDF file. The Import section lets you upload previously exported archives or individual .md/.txt files.
howto_settings_text: In Settings you can change your theme, switch language, manage reflection prompt categories, create custom scales and tags, export or import data, and change your password.
date_format_desc: Choose how dates are displayed throughout the app.
sticky_note_desc: A personal message shown at the top of every page. Use it for reminders, quotes, or anything you want to see every time you open the app.

help_intro: Welcome! This guide walks you through everything DailyMood can do — from your first entry to habit trackers and the CBT reference. Read it end to end or jump to whatever you need; the table of contents below will take you there.
help_gs_intro: DailyMood is your private journal: it runs on your own machine, everything is encrypted, and nothing ever leaves your network. Here's how to settle in.
help_gs_bullet_account: Create your account — pick a username and a password, and answer the security question. That answer is your safety net: it can recover your entries if you ever forget your password.
help_gs_bullet_first: Write your first entry — open New Entry in the top bar, jot down how the day went, rate your mood, and save. That's it; there is no wrong way to keep a journal.
help_gs_bullet_where: What lives where — the Journal is your calendar home; Insights brings together charts and search; Free Write is a notebook for longer writing; Trackers keeps your habits; and Settings holds everything you can tune. This Help page is always one click away in the top bar.
help_gs_bullet_profile: Make it yours — choose language, theme, accent color, and date format in Settings, and write a Sticky Note with a personal message that greets you on every page.
help_journal_intro: The calendar is the heart of the app: each day can hold an entry with a mood, text, tags, and your custom scale values. Days are colored by mood, so patterns tend to jump out at you.
help_journal_mood: Moods go from 0 to 6 — from a very hard day to a fantastic one. Slide the mood picker to whatever fits; there are no wrong answers.
help_journal_text: Entries are just for you — write freely in the entry body. Everything is encrypted before it touches the disk.
help_journal_tags: Tags — add short labels like work, family, or sleep to see how different parts of your life line up with your mood. Tags are stored per language, so they always match the app language you are using.
help_journal_scales: Custom scales — define your own numeric scales in Settings (for example Anxiety 0–10 or Energy 1–5) and record a value for each on any entry. Perfect for tracking what a single mood number cannot capture.
help_journal_prompts: Reflection prompts — optionally turn on guided questions while writing. Prompts span eight categories (gratitude, growth, emotions, and more); choose which categories appear in Settings. Answer honestly — there are no right answers.
help_journal_edit: Editing — click a day in the calendar to see its entry, then edit or delete it whenever you like. You can also write entries for past days.
help_journal_sticky: Sticky Note — a personal message shown at the top of every page. Use it for a mantra, a reminder, or anything you want to see often.
help_freewrite_intro: Sometimes a dated entry is too small for what you need to say. Free Write is a notebook-style space for long, unstructured writing.
help_freewrite_sessions: Sessions — create as many free writes as you like, each with its own title. Think of them as pages in a notebook rather than days in a diary.
help_freewrite_autosave: Autosave — your writing is saved as you type, so there is nothing to remember and nothing to lose.
help_freewrite_words: Word count — a live counter keeps you company as you write.
help_freewrite_export: Export — download a single session or all of them as a formatted PDF whenever you want a copy outside the app.
help_insights_intro: Insights brings your entries, filters, and charts together on one page, so you can see how you have been doing and dig into why.
help_insights_filters: Filters — narrow everything by tags and by date range. The filters apply to the entry list and the charts alike.
help_insights_charts: Charts — mood over time, mood distribution, mood by day of week, mood by tag, and your most used tags. Together they answer questions like "are my weekends really better?" or "which tag pulls my mood down?"
help_insights_totals: At a glance — total entries, current streak, and longest streak sit at the top. Streaks count consecutive days with an entry.
help_insights_pdf: PDF export — compile the numbers and charts into a stats PDF, or export the entries themselves. Handy for sharing with a therapist.
help_trackers_intro: Trackers come in two flavors: one measures the time since you last did something you are staying away from, the other counts occurrences of something you want to understand. Both live under Trackers.
help_trackers_timer_text: The withdraw timer shows how long it has been since the last occurrence, ticking in real time — days, hours, minutes, seconds. Set the last occurrence when you create it (or fix it later), add a motivational note to remind yourself why you are doing this, and press "I did it again" if you slip — the timer restarts honestly. Your longest run is kept alongside, so one setback never erases what you have already achieved.
help_trackers_counter_text: The behavior counter logs every occurrence of a habit or symptom — anxiety crises, cigarettes, nail biting, anything you want to count. Each time you log one, four quick questions capture the context: What were you doing? How were you feeling? What was on your mind? What were the possible triggers? You can backdate an occurrence too. The card shows your all-time total and today's count.
help_trackers_patterns_text: Under each counter, the Patterns view groups your history into occurrences per day and your most frequent triggers. This is where the real insight lives: if you track anxiety crises, for example, you may notice they cluster on certain days and that one trigger — work meetings, poor sleep, conflict — keeps showing up. Naming the pattern is the first step to changing it, and the data makes a great starting point for a conversation with a therapist.
help_reminders_intro: A gentle nudge when the day is almost over and today's entry is still missing. Reminders come in two levels, and both are entirely under your control.
help_reminders_banner: In-app nudge — when you open the app and have not written today, a small banner appears at the top with a shortcut to a new entry. If a streak is on the line, it says so. You can dismiss it at any time.
help_reminders_ntfy: Push notifications (optional) — disabled by default. To enable them, turn on the daily reminder in Settings and point it at an ntfy server: the server URL (a self-hosted instance is the most private choice), the time and timezone for the daily push, a severity from 1 (silent) to 5 (urgent), and optionally an access token for your topic.
help_reminders_privacy: Privacy — only a generic reminder message is ever sent to the notification server. The contents of your journal, your moods, and your streak counts never leave your machine.
help_privacy_intro: DailyMood is built so that your journal stays yours. Here is what protects it.
help_privacy_encryption: Encrypted at rest — every entry is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it is written to disk, using a unique key per user. Stolen files are unreadable without your password.
help_privacy_offline: 100% offline — no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics, no third-party services. The app talks only to your own server.
help_privacy_devices: Remembered devices — stay logged in on devices you trust and pick "Continue as [you]" on the login screen next time. Manage or forget devices anytime in Settings; changing your password revokes all of them.
help_privacy_pin: Device PIN — an optional 4–8 digit shortcut on remembered devices. It is a convenience layer with brute-force lockout; your password remains the primary login, and the PIN itself is never stored.
help_privacy_reset: Password recovery — your security question can recover your entries even if the password is gone. Resetting your password keeps your journal intact but signs out every remembered device.
help_privacy_backup: Export & backup — export everything as plain .md files inside an archive, import archives back, or generate PDFs. Your journal also lives as simple files in the directories you control: back up your entries and data folders and you are safe.
help_sec_cbt_title: A guide to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
help_cbt_intro: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy — CBT, or TCC in Portuguese — offers a practical map of how thoughts, feelings, and behaviors feed one another, and how to interrupt the cycle. This guide collects the 12 most common cognitive distortions with everyday examples. Keep it nearby while you journal: spotting a distortion in your own writing is already half the work.
help_cbt_closing: Notice a distortion in your entry? Name it kindly — "that's catastrophizing" — and try writing a more balanced version of the thought right next to it. No self-criticism required; these patterns are human.

mindmap_intro: Sketch your thoughts as branches or rings — private, calm, and yours alone.
mindmap_kind_mindmap_desc: A classic tree that grows outward from a core idea, branches left and right.
mindmap_kind_radial_desc: Concentric rings — each tier wraps the core, great for layered themes.
mindmap_relation_hint: Relation mode: click another node to connect it.
mindmap_delete_confirm: Delete this node and everything under it?
mindmap_delete_map_confirm: Delete this map and all its nodes?
mindmap_empty: A place for thoughts to branch out
mindmap_empty_desc: Mind maps grow outward from one core idea; radial maps wrap each layer in rings. Start with whichever feels right — you can't get it wrong.
